messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Diplomat
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 66

# A Diplomat's Return

Arjun sits in the embassy's climate-controlled conference room, reviewing trade agreements with the same meticulous attention he's always brought to his work. His colleagues consider him one of the most promising members of the South Asian desk—articulate, culturally attuned, fluent in three languages. They don't notice how his leg bounces beneath the table, or how his eyes keep tracking the door. They certainly don't know that two years ago, he was in Beirut when the explosions started.

He had been there as a junior diplomat, a posting he'd fought hard for at twenty-two. It was supposed to be a straightforward assignment—cultural liaison work, attending community events, building relationships. On a Tuesday morning in March, he was walking to a café near the embassy when the first blast hit three blocks away. The sound was unlike anything he'd ever experienced—not just loud, but physical, a force that seemed to reorganize his entire body. He remembers the windows shattering around him, the taste of concrete dust, the smell of burning plastic and something else he still can't identify. He remembers running, though he's not sure where he was running to. He remembers a woman's hand gripping his arm, pulling him into a building, both of them pressed against a wall while the sounds continued outside.

The official report called it a car bombing. Twenty-three people died. Arjun wasn't injured physically, so he stayed in Beirut for another three months to finish his posting. Everyone praised his composure, his commitment. He told himself he was fine.

Now, back in his home country, he's learning that "fine" is a complicated word.

Sleep has become something he negotiates with rather than experiences. He'll lie beside his girlfriend, Priya, staring at the ceiling until three or four in the morning, his mind replaying scenarios that didn't happen. Sometimes he dreams he's back in that building, but the exits are sealed. Other times, the blast happens while he's at the embassy, and he watches colleagues buried under rubble. He wakes with his heart hammering so hard he thinks it might break through his ribs. Priya has stopped asking if he's okay because she's learned that the answer is always yes, even when his hands are shaking.

During the day, his hypervigilance disguises itself as professionalism. He's acutely aware of every person who enters a room, every sound in the hallway, every potential exit. He's mapped escape routes in the embassy without consciously deciding to do so. When a colleague dropped a stack of files last week, Arjun flinched so violently that he knocked over his coffee. He made a joke about it—something about being clumsy—and everyone laughed. But his heart was racing for twenty minutes afterward.

What troubles him most are the moments when he's supposed to feel normal. Priya wanted to go to a concert last month, and he agreed because he's supposed to want these things. But sitting in the crowded venue, surrounded by the press of bodies and the unpredictable noise, he felt a suffocating panic rising in his chest. He excused himself to the bathroom and sat in a stall for fifteen minutes, breathing deliberately, reminding himself he was safe. He didn't tell Priya why he left early.

His work remains impeccable. He's been asked to lead a delegation next month. He'll say yes. He'll prepare thoroughly. And he'll manage the low-level terror that accompanies any assignment involving travel, any situation he cannot completely control. He's learned to compartmentalize so well that sometimes he almost believes his own performance. Almost.
